name: Angular gyrus
summary: The posterior part of the inferior parietal lobule, arching over the end of the superior temporal sulcus at the meeting point of the parietal, temporal and occipital lobes. It is a multimodal hub: on the dominant side it links written symbols with language (reading, writing), numbers with quantity (calculation) and the body with its labels (finger recognition, right-left), so a left angular lesion yields Gerstmann syndrome and alexia with agraphia. On the right it contributes to spatial attention and self-location, and stimulation here produces out-of-body experiences.

anatomy.location: Behind the supramarginal gyrus at the posterior end of the superior temporal sulcus, bordering the occipital lobe; the angular artery of the MCA reaches it as the artery's terminal branch.

function: Reading, writing, calculation, finger gnosis, right-left orientation, semantic integration and, on the right, spatial attention and body awareness.

bestView.label: angular gyrus at the temporo-parieto-occipital junction
gyrus over the end of the superior temporal sulcus

imaging.normalAppearance: Lies at the posterior end of the superior temporal sulcus, in the MCA–PCA watershed; infarcts and posterior cortical atrophy involve it early.

pathology.finding: Left temporoparietal restriction with Gerstmann syndrome and alexia with agraphia.
Wedge at the MCA–PCA boundary involving the angular gyrus after hypotension.

lesionEffects.deficit: Gerstmann syndrome: acalculia, agraphia, finger agnosia, right-left disorientation

lesionEffects.mechanism: Disconnection of visual word forms from language

examination: Write a sentence, read a paragraph
Serial sevens and simple written arithmetic
Name and point to fingers; show right hand, left ear
pearls: Complete Gerstmann syndrome is rare; any two components with an inferior quadrantanopia point to the left angular gyrus
Alexia with agraphia (angular) differs from alexia without agraphia (occipital plus splenium)
